title: Viewing a Binary Tree From the Right Side

phrases.phrase: looking at it from the right side
phrases.explanation: Imagining you are standing to the right of the tree and observing which nodes are visible
Processing the tree one depth at a time, from top to bottom

phrases.phrase: let me walk through an example
phrases.explanation: A common phrase meaning to trace through a specific case step by step
Acknowledging understanding of the explanation or approach
Highlighting the most important idea behind an approach

technical_terms.definition: A tree data structure where each node has at most two children, called left and right
Breadth-First Search, a traversal that visits all nodes at the current depth before moving deeper
Depth-First Search, a traversal that goes as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking
A first-in-first-out data structure often used for BFS traversal
A technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems

concept: Given the root of a binary tree, return the values of the nodes that are visible when looking at the tree from the right side, ordered from top to bottom.

solutions.label: BFS Level Order (Collect Last)
solutions.summary: Use BFS to traverse level by level, collecting the last node at each level.

solutions.label: DFS Right-First Recursion
solutions.summary: Use DFS visiting right child first, recording the first node seen at each new depth.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["1"]:::red --> B["2"]
    A --> C["3"]:::red
    B --> D["5"]:::red
    B --> E[" "]
    C --> F[" "]
    C --> G["4"]:::red
    classDef red fill:#f87171,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    style E fill:none,stroke:none
    style F fill:none,stroke:none

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given a binary tree, and I want you to imagine standing on the right side of it. Return the values of the nodes you can see from that perspective, ordered top to bottom.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: So I need to find the rightmost visible node at each level of the tree. Could the tree be empty?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the tree can be empty, in which case return an empty list. The tree can have up to a few thousand nodes, and node values are integers.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. And the rightmost visible node isn't always the right child, correct? If a left child exists at a deeper level with no right sibling, it would be visible too.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. For example, consider a tree with root one, left child two, right child three, and node two has a left child five, and node three has a right child four. The right side view would be one, three, four.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: That makes sense. So the answer is the last node at each depth. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: BFS Level Order Traversal
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph "Level 0"
    A["1"]:::blue
    end
    subgraph "Level 1"
    B["2"]
    C["3"]:::blue
    end
    subgraph "Level 2"
    D["5"]
    G["4"]:::blue
    end
    A --> B
    A --> C
    B --> D
    C --> G
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is to use BFS with a queue. I process the tree level by level, and at each level, I record the last node I encounter. That last node is the one visible from the right.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Starting with node one in the queue. Level zero has one node, so the last node is one. Next, I add two and three. Level one has two nodes, and the last is three. Then I process two's child five and three's child four. Level two ends with four. The result is one, three, four.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time and space complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n since I visit every node once. Space is O of n because in the worst case the queue holds an entire level, which could be up to n over two nodes in a complete tree.

sections.title: DFS Right-First Recursion
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["1 depth=0"]:::purple -->|"visit 2nd"| B["2 depth=1"]
    A -->|"visit 1st"| C["3 depth=1"]:::purple
    B --> D["5 depth=2"]
    C --> G["4 depth=2"]:::purple
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We can improve space usage with DFS. The key insight is: if I visit the right child before the left child, the first node I see at each new depth is the rightmost one. I track the current depth and only add a value when I reach a depth I haven't recorded yet.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How does that look on our example?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I start at node one, depth zero. The result list is empty so I add one. Then I go right to node three at depth one. The list has one entry so depth one is new, I add three. Then right child of three is four at depth two, which is new, so I add four. When I backtrack and visit left subtrees, depths zero, one, and two are already recorded, so nothing more is added.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is still O of n since we visit every node. But space improves to O of h where h is the height of the tree. For a balanced tree that's O of log n, which is better than the BFS approach.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison
    BFS["BFS Level Order\nTime: O of n\nSpace: O of n"]:::blue
    DFS["DFS Right-First\nTime: O of n\nSpace: O of h"]:::purple
    end
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#333,color:#fff
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#333,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. Both approaches visit every node in O of n time. The BFS approach is intuitive and uses a queue with O of n space. The DFS approach is more space-efficient at O of h by visiting the right side first.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Right. For balanced trees, DFS saves space. BFS might be easier to explain in an interview since the level-by-level logic is straightforward. Both are solid choices.
